RBP REST API enhancements

PLA-58003

Changed

Minor

Automatically on

 

Facts in this post come from SAP’s 2H 2026 release notes (latest revision 2 October 2026). Anything labelled Suggested is my recommendation, not SAP’s.

 

1. Proxy: creating proxies and acting as a proxy are now separate permissions

Before: Holding Proxy Management did two jobs. It gave access to the Proxy Management UI to create proxy assignments for the target population. It also let the holder act on behalf of their entire target population for all proxy modules, without an explicit 1:1 proxy assignment. There was no option to restrict proxy access to specific modules in RBP.

Now: The two jobs are separate permissions.

 

Permission

What it does now

Proxy Management

Gives access to the Proxy Management UI to create assignments for the target population.

Proxy Rights (under General User Permission)

Lets administrators act on behalf of their target population for the selected proxy modules. Also used to create group-to-group proxy assignments.

 

When you define a Proxy Rights permission role in Admin Center > Manage Permission Roles, you set:

  • Access Population: the users who will act as proxy.
  • Target Population: the users the access population can proxy into.
  • Proxy Modules: all modules or a selected subset, shown in a parent-child hierarchy. Selecting a child module automatically includes its parent.

What happens at release: To avoid disruption, anyone holding Proxy Management at release is automatically granted Proxy Rights with all modules selected. No manual migration step is required. To narrow a role, open it in Manage Permission Roles and update the proxy module selection under the Proxy Rights settings.

Watch-outs from the release note:

  • Selecting the Reporting proxy module or its sub-modules gives the proxy access to all reports. Selecting Performance Management Forms gives access to all Performance Management forms. For more granular control of reports and forms, use the Proxy Management admin tool.
  • To act as a proxy, a user needs either Proxy Rights or an explicit 1:1 proxy assignment created through the Proxy Management tool. When both apply, the explicit 1:1 assignment takes priority.
  • To open the Proxy Management UI, you need the Proxy Management permission in your role.

Why it matters: SAP’s own summary is that you can now give specific administrators access to the proxy management UI without also granting them proxy access.

Suggested: Because the automatic grant is all modules, list everyone who holds Proxy Management and decide who needs all modules, some modules or no proxy rights.

 

2. More MDF objects are secured by default

Before: For these objects, the Access to non-secured objects permission was necessary to view, create and update records. All users who held it could also add and delete objects.

Now: From 2H 2026, eight MDF objects are delivered as secured by default. SAP states that it is not possible to change this setting:

  • Position
  • Position Type
  • Position Right to Return
  • Position Requisition Mapping
  • Position Job Requisition Processing Request
  • Position Requisition Status
  • Company Structure Definition
  • Company Structure UI Configuration

What happens to your existing roles depends on where you started:

 

Your situation

What happens

You had already secured the object

No change

The object was not secured, and the role does not have Access to non-secured objects

No change

The object was not secured, but the role does have Access to non-secured objects

The system grants the role permissions on the object from the new User > Position Management Object Permissions category

 

Two objects from 1H 2026 were also re-documented in this release “for clarity”. They follow the same three-way logic, but the grants go to different categories:

 

Object

Delivered

Where the system grants permissions

Hire Date Correction

1H 2026

Manage Data category: Object-Level Permissions, View, Edit, Import, Export, View Pending Approvals and Review Pending Approvals. The release note says there are no changes to permissions granted in the “Manager User” category.

Fallback Event Reason Configuration

1H 2026

Administrator > Manage Business Configuration category

 

Why SAP made the change: It is part of a general initiative to make all unsecured MDF objects secure by default, so customers make informed decisions on which target groups they provide appropriate permissions to.

Suggested: List the roles that hold Access to non-secured objects and open each in Manage Permission Roles. Review the permissions the system granted under Position Management Object Permissions, Manage Data and Manage Business Configuration. The old permission allowed adding and deleting, so check what the new grants allow and remove anything the role doesn’t need.

 

3. Learning admin roles can now be assigned through RBP

Learning administrator roles can now be assigned in Admin Center > Manage Permission Roles, in addition to the existing standalone Learning role assignment function. In Step 2 (Add Permissions), roles appear as dynamic child permissions under a new permission, Learning Administrator Role Assignment.

How it works:

  • The child permissions are synced from Learning. When Learning admin roles are added or removed in Learning, the child permissions update after the automatically triggered Refresh RBP Model job completes.
  • After you assign the permission to administrators, a daily job, Sync Learning Admin Role Access to Learning, syncs those administrators to Learning. The job runs in delta mode automatically. If you see data inconsistencies, you can trigger a full sync manually in Scheduled Job Manager.
  • If the admin user doesn’t exist in Learning, they are created automatically during role assignment.
  • Assignment and revocation are reflected in Learning within approximately 15 minutes of the sync job completing. Changes are not immediate.
  • Changes to permission groups, such as adding or removing members, are reflected in Learning after the sync job runs.
  • You don’t need to grant Learning admin roles in both RBP and Learning. Managing them through RBP is sufficient.

Rules in the role editor:

  • Selecting only Learning Admin Access Permission, without a role under Learning Administrator Role Assignment, shows an informational message.
  • Selecting Learning Administrator Role Assignment and at least one role selects Learning Admin Access Permission automatically.
  • Unselecting Learning Admin Access Permission also unselects Learning Administrator Role Assignment and resets the dropdown.
  • Selecting Learning Administrator Role Assignment without choosing a role shows an error asking you to provide values for the highlighted fields.

Prerequisite: Learning must be installed in integrated and sealed mode and run version 2H 2026 or higher. If Learning isn’t integrated, is integrated but not sealed, or runs an earlier version, a warning appears in Manage Permission Roles and Learning administrator roles are not shown or available for assignment. SAP points to KBA 3193649 for sealing your Learning instance.

Person mode: If Learning has Person mode enabled, a user may not be removed from the Learning admin role even after the corresponding child permission in RBP is removed. SAP says this is expected, not a bug, and occurs when the same person has another active employment that retains the role.

To verify: In Learning Administration > System Administration > Security > Role Management, open an administrator role and check the Users tab.

 

4. RBP change audit reports now come in two versions

You create the reports as before, in Admin Center > Change Audit Reports > Create Configuration Data Report. The Access Reports tab then shows two versions of each report, for example RBP_GROUP_CHANGE_REPORT and RBP_GROUP_CHANGE_REPORT_V2. V2 has additional data fields, broader audit coverage and faster data availability. It is available for four report types:

 

Report

Major enhancements in V2

RBP Group Change Report

For the Group name field, the original captured only updates to existing names. V2 also covers creation and deletion.

RBP Static Group Membership Change Report

Adds a Display Name column showing the user’s display name.

RBP Role Change Report

Splits Permission into three fields: Permission (standard RBP permissions), Advanced Permission (resource-based permissions that require target criteria during setup) and MDF Permission (Metadata Framework permissions).

 

Splits Role Assignment into Role Assignment Basic Details and Advanced Permission Target Criteria. The new Basic Details field covers permission data blocking information.

 

Splits Group into MDF Permission Basic Target Criteria, MDF Permission Basic Data Blocking and MDF Permission Target Criteria for Position.

 

Adds new fields such as Role Description and RBP-Only.

RBP User Role Change Report

Renames RuleId to Role Assignment ID for clearer identification. The Context 4 Key and Context 4 Value columns, unused in the original report, now show the user’s display name.

(Figure 1:  V2 version of RBP reports)

Prerequisite: Change audit logging must be enabled for your system.

Two behaviors to plan for:

1. V2 may contain more data than the original. It is built on a new audit technology that makes data available faster, so when both reports are generated at the same time, V2 may hold more.

(Figure 2: RBP Group Change Report)

(Figure 3: RBP Role Change Report )

 

2. Audit Log Service can return two sets of records per change. If you access RBP change audit data through SAP Audit Log

Service, the payload may contain one set from the new technology and one from the original. Records from the new technology appear sooner, so a query shortly after a change may return only those, and the original records may arrive later. Check the objectType field in the payload to tell them apart. SAP’s Module-Specific Fields, Attribute Names and Coded Values page explains how to identify records from the new technology.

The release note does not say how long both versions will be offered.

Suggested: Make one permission change, generate both reports and keep the comparison as evidence. Tell anyone who consumes Audit Log Service data that each change may appear twice.

 

5. Hide Story report data for forms that never reached a user’s Inbox

A user with Data Access: Story can view Performance Management data in Story reports for all forms matching the selected form templates and target population. That can include forms that never reached their Inbox and are probably irrelevant to them. SAP’s example is Ask for Feedback requests and replies for forms they weren’t involved in.

The new permission Hide Story Report Data for Forms Never in Inbox (User Permissions > Performance) prevents users from seeing that data. It works together with Data Access: Story and is disabled by default. SAP says it helps ensure data privacy and relevance in Performance Management Story reports.

Requirements:

  • Story reports are enabled.
  • Enable Performance Management Access Permission is selected in the Performance Management Feature Settings admin tool.
  • Users are granted Performance > Data Access: Story.

Suggested: Review who holds Data Access: Story and decide whether they should see data for forms that never reached their Inbox. If not, grant the new permission.

 

6. REST API enhancements

  • POST /assignments now returns an id field for the created assignment, so you no longer need a follow-up GET request. Previously it returned only a 201 Created status code.
  • POST /roles and PUT /roles now support an externalCode field for MDF permissions in both requests and responses. For requests involving MDF permissions, you must provide either the MDF entity’s externalCode or its resourceId. The external code applies only to MDF permissions (resource type MDF_OBJECT), not to other resource-based permissions.

SAP will update the API documentation on SAP Business Accelerator Hub (SAP SuccessFactors Role-Based Permission Management API) on the Valid as Of date, 13 November 2026.

Sample Code 
"resources": [
    {
      "resourceId": 111,
      "externalCode": "obj4qaBEDataSource", //External code of the MDF resource. Only applicable when resourceType is MDF_OBJECT.
      "resourceType": "MDF_OBJECT",
      "selectedActions": [
        {
          "name": "VIEW_HISTORY"
        } ...

Suggested: If you manage roles or assignments through scripts or integrations, check that MDF permission requests supply externalCode or resourceId. You can also use the returned assignment id instead of a follow-up GET.

 

Pre-release checklist (suggested)

 

#

Action

Related change

1

List everyone holding Proxy Management. They will receive Proxy Rights for all modules. Decide who should be narrowed.

Proxy

2

Identify roles holding Access to non-secured objects and review the grants the system added (Position Management Object Permissions, Manage Data, Manage Business Configuration).

MDF

3

Confirm Learning is integrated, sealed and on 2H 2026 or higher. Agree whether RBP becomes the single place to manage Learning admins.

Learning

4

Run the original and V2 reports after one test change. Decide which version is your evidence of record.

Audit

5

Tell consumers of Audit Log Service data about duplicate record sets and the objectType field.

Audit

6

Decide whether to grant Hide Story Report Data for Forms Never in Inbox, and to whom.

Story

7

Check integrations that call POST /assignments or POST/PUT /roles.

API

8

Update control descriptions and screenshots in your audit documentation.

Audit

 

Suggested tests

 

Test

What to confirm

Grant Proxy Management only (no Proxy Rights, no 1:1 assignment) to a test user

User can open the Proxy Management UI but cannot act as proxy

Define a Proxy Rights role with one child module

Proxy can act in that module and its parent. Check the Reporting and Performance Management Forms behavior.

Open a role that held Access to non-secured objects

New grants appear under Position Management Object Permissions, and you can explain each one

Assign a Learning admin role through RBP

Admin appears in Learning (Role Management > Users tab) about 15 minutes after the sync job completes

Change an MDF permission and a role assignment, then run both reports

The change appears in the V2 split fields (MDF Permission, Role Assignment Basic Details, Advanced Permission Target Criteria)

Make one change and query Audit Log Service twice, shortly after and later

Count the record sets and use objectType to separate new from original records

Grant the Story hiding permission to a test user

Data for forms never in their Inbox no longer appears in Story reports

Call POST /assignments

Response includes id

Create or update a role with an MDF permission via POST/PUT /roles

Request accepts externalCode or resourceId, and the response includes externalCode

 

Closing thought

 

Four of these changes tighten control or evidence. Proxy Rights separates managing proxies from being one, the MDF change secures more objects, V2 gives finer audit fields, and the Story permission lets you hide data for forms users never received. The Learning change centralizes administration in RBP, and the API change makes automation easier.

Two changes also act on your roles automatically: the Proxy Rights grant and the Position Management grants. SAP designed them to avoid disruption, so they carry over the access your roles already had. That is our reading, not SAP’s, but it is why both deserve a review before 13 November.

Disclaimer: Test every change in your preview environment before it reaches production, and validate it against your own role and permission design. SAP can change its release notes at any time, and this post reflects them as last revised on 2 October 2026. Always check the SAP SuccessFactors What’s New Viewer for the latest updates.

entry.title: AI‑Guided Desired Vendor in ME51N — explainable supplier recommendation in the Purchase Requisition
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 1 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". This part: the in‑transaction assistant. Part 2: the SAP BTP + AI Core "brain". Part 3: the standalone RAP + Fiori app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

Prerequisites (prototype). Part 1 needs SAP S/4HANA (ABAP Platform) with the classic ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST BAdI. The standalone app in Part 3 uses ABAP RAP (managed, draft‑enabled BO — recent ABAP Platform / S/4HANA 2020+). The recommendation service (Part 2) runs on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry and calls SAP AI Core (generative‑AI hub / orchestration; this prototype uses gpt‑4o‑mini). Exact minimum releases depend on your landscape — verify before you build.

TL;DR

Buyers pick the Desired Vendor on a purchase requisition mostly from memory — while the delivery‑performance data that should drive that choice sits unused in S/4. We put an explainable AI recommendation right into ME51N: the moment a material is entered, the Desired Vendor is defaulted to the AI‑recommended supplier, and a top‑5 popup shows each candidate with its reason and a confidence rating. It's built with a supported BAdI (no modification, no rebuild), it's safe (the AI can never invent a vendor and only aggregated KPIs leave S/4), and the very same enhancement shows up in the "Purchase Requisition – Advanced" Fiori app for free.

ME51N showing the AI supplier recommendation popup with top 5 suppliers

The problem: a decision made from memory

Open ME51N, add an item, and you hit the Desired Vendor field. For a material with several historical suppliers, which one actually delivered on time last year? Which short‑shipped? The answer lives in your purchase‑order and goods‑receipt history — but no buyer has time to query that mid‑transaction. So the field gets filled by habit: the vendor we used last time, or the name we recognize. Multiply that by thousands of requisitions and you have a steady drip of avoidable delivery risk and missed consolidation — invisible, because nothing ever flagged it.

The data to choose better already exists. It just isn't where the decision is made.

This is a small, concrete example of AI in S/4HANA done in the spirit of SAP's Business AI principles — relevant, reliable, responsible — but as a custom extension on SAP's own AI platform (SAP AI Core), not out‑of‑the‑box functionality: the intelligence runs inside the SAP landscape, and only aggregated KPIs ever leave S/4.

What we built, at a glance

When a buyer enters a material (and quantity/plant) in ME51N:

  • Desired Vendor auto‑fills with the AI‑recommended supplier — but only when the field is empty and the AI is confident enough.
  • A top‑5 popup lists the recommended supplier plus alternatives, each with the AI's reason and an overall confidence rating. The buyer can accept the default or double‑click another.
  • Every decision — what the AI recommended vs. what the buyer chose — is logged for adoption analytics.
  • A config table switches the whole thing on/off per plant / purchasing group.

AI-filled Desired Vendor

Why put it in ME51N (instead of a new app)

The instinct is to build a shiny new Fiori app. But the buyer already lives in ME51N — the highest‑ value place for a recommendation is the field they're about to fill, not a separate screen they'd have to remember to open. So we enhanced the transaction itself, using the ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST BAdI — a supported extension point, no modification.

The bonus: the "Purchase Requisition – Advanced" Fiori app is the same enjoy transaction rendered in SAP GUI for HTML. Because we enhanced the backend, the recommendation and the popup appear in that Fiori app too, with no extra UI work.

Pattern — inject an AI recommendation into a classic transaction, safely This approach generalizes far beyond procurement. To add AI to almost any classic SAP transaction:

  1. Find a supported BAdI at item/save time (here, ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST~PROCESS_ITEM).
  2. Fetch from a cached helper — never call an external service on every dialog roundtrip.
  3. Default only when the field is empty and the AI is confident — assist, don't override.
  4. Make it explainable and actionable — show the reasons; let the user choose.
  5. Gate and audit — config kill switch + a decision log. Swap the field and the BAdI, and the same skeleton works for account assignment, delivery dates, incoterms — anywhere a data‑driven default helps.

Responsible AI, by design

This only works if buyers trust it — so the guardrails aren't an afterthought, they're the design:

  • Human‑in‑the‑loop — the AI defaults a value; the buyer always decides. Nothing is posted behind their back.
  • Explainable — every supplier carries a plain‑language reason and a confidence rating, shown in the popup. No black box.
  • No invented vendors — the AI may only rank/justify suppliers we already sent it; the service rejects anything else (more in Part 2).
  • Data minimization — only aggregated KPIs leave S/4; no raw PO/GR history.
  • Graceful degradation — if the AI is unavailable it falls back to the best supplier by history (flagged BASELINE) and never blocks the transaction; a config flag can switch it off entirely.

How it works (technical deep‑dive)

From here on it's for the developers. If you're here for the concept, skip to “What's next”.

The architecture: deterministic ABAP + a guarded LLM

The trick to trustworthy AI in a transaction is to keep the facts deterministic and keep the AI on a short leash. ABAP computes the hard numbers — on‑time rate, fill rate, delay, a baseline score and rank — from real history, and hands the AI only a shortlist of eligible candidates. The AI's job is narrow: rank and explain within that shortlist. It never sees raw history and can't add a supplier.


The BAdI lifecycle

We implement three methods of ME_PROCESS_REQ_CUST (ZME_REQ_AISUP_DEFAULT); everything else stays empty:

  • INITIALIZE — a new requisition starts: reset the per‑PR cache and buffers.
  • PROCESS_ITEM — the workhorse (fires on every roundtrip, per item): default the vendor, offer the popup, buffer the decision.
  • POST — on save: write the audit log.

Here's the core of PROCESS_ITEM (trimmed):

METHOD if_ex_me_process_req_cust~process_item.
  " Only during PR creation. (Confirm the advanced Fiori app's tcode via System → Status.)
  IF sy-tcode <> 'ME51N'.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.

  DATA(ls_item) = im_item->get_data( ).
  IF ls_item-matnr IS INITIAL.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.

  " Config-driven kill switch / overwrite / min-confidence per plant + purchasing group.
  DATA(ls_cfg) = zcl_aisup_pr_default=>get_config( iv_plant = ls_item-werks iv_ekgrp = ls_item-ekgrp ).
  IF ls_cfg-enabled = abap_false.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.

  " Cached: the external service is called at most once per material/plant per PR.
  DATA(ls_reco) = zcl_aisup_pr_default=>get_recommendation( iv_material = ls_item-matnr
                                                            iv_plant    = ls_item-werks ).

  " (a) Auto-default: only when confident AND the field is still empty.
  IF ls_reco-vendor IS NOT INITIAL
     AND zcl_aisup_pr_default=>conf_ge( iv_conf = ls_reco-confidence iv_min = ls_cfg-min_conf )
     AND ( ls_item-lifnr IS INITIAL OR ls_cfg-overwrite = abap_true ).
    ls_item-lifnr = ls_reco-vendor.        " LIFNR = Desired Vendor
    im_item->set_data( ls_item ).
  ENDIF.

  " (b) Explainable, actionable popup — once per line item.
  IF ls_item-menge > 0 AND ls_item-werks IS NOT INITIAL.
    DATA(lv_chosen) = zcl_aisup_pr_default=>show_popup( iv_item_id = ls_item-bnfpo is_reco = ls_reco ).
    IF lv_chosen IS NOT INITIAL.
      ls_item = im_item->get_data( ).
      ls_item-lifnr = lv_chosen.
      im_item->set_data( ls_item ).
    ENDIF.
  ENDIF.

  " (c) Buffer the decision for the audit log (flushed on POST).
  ls_item = im_item->get_data( ).
  zcl_aisup_pr_default=>buffer_decision( iv_item_id = ls_item-bnfpo iv_matnr = ls_item-matnr
                                         iv_plant   = ls_item-werks iv_chosen = ls_item-lifnr
                                         is_reco    = ls_reco ).
ENDMETHOD.

Three design decisions worth calling out:

  • Performance: PROCESS_ITEM fires on every screen roundtrip, so a synchronous HTTP call each time would wreck the dialog. The helper caches per material/plant, so the service is hit at most once per material — the popup and defaulting are then instant.
  • Assist, don't override: we fill only when the field is empty (unless config says otherwise), so a buyer's manual entry is never clobbered.
  • Confidence gate: the silent auto‑fill happens only above a configured confidence; below that, we still show the popup but leave the field for the buyer.

The explainable popup (and an ALV gotcha)

The popup is a classic ALV selection (REUSE_ALV_POPUP_TO_SELECT) — which, handily, renders in both SAP GUI and the WebGUI‑based advanced Fiori app. One catch: classic ALV cells can't wrap text, and AI reasons are long. The fix is to split a long reason across extra rows (only the first row of a supplier carries rank/name/confidence) and keep a hidden supplier‑index column so selecting any row still resolves to the right vendor.

" wrap a long reason across rows; SUP_IDX (hidden) maps any row back to its supplier
DO.
  DATA(lv_len) = COND i( WHEN strlen( lv_rest ) > lc_wrap THEN lc_wrap ELSE strlen( lv_rest ) ).
  APPEND VALUE #( rank    = COND #( WHEN lv_first = abap_true THEN |{ ls_sup-rank }| ELSE '' )
                  reason  = COND #( WHEN lv_len > 0 THEN lv_rest+0(lv_len) ELSE '' )
                  sup_idx = lv_idx ) TO lt_disp.
  lv_first = abap_false.
  IF strlen( lv_rest ) > lc_wrap. lv_rest = lv_rest+lc_wrap. ELSE. EXIT. ENDIF.
ENDDO.

Top-5 suppliers, each with an AI reason and confidence

Gotchas we hit (so you don't have to)

  • IS_PERSISTENT( ) isn't public on IF_PURCHASE_REQUISITION_ITEM — so we gate create‑mode on sy-tcode rather than item state. (Confirm the advanced app's transaction with System → Status.)
  • abap_boolean is not valid in a DDIC table definition — use abap.char(1) for flag columns (it still compares fine against abap_true/abap_false in code).
  • REUSE_ALV_POPUP_TO_SELECT needs I_TABNAME — omit it and you get a CALL_FUNCTION_PARM_MISSING short dump at runtime, not a syntax error.

Measurable value (and how we'll prove it)

Because every line's decision — AI pick vs. what the buyer chose, with confidence and reason — is written to an audit table on save, we don't have to assert value; we can measure it: AI‑pick acceptance rate, override rate, and confidence distribution, straight from the log.

  Before After (measurable target)

Vendor chosen bymemory / habitranked history + explained AI pick
Time to a defensible choiceminutes (or skipped)seconds, in‑transaction
"Why this vendor?""we always do"on‑time / fill / delay, in writing
Governanceinvisibleevery decision logged

What's next

That's the buyer‑facing half. But how does it decide — without hallucinating a supplier? In Part 2 we open up the brain: the SAP BTP microservice and SAP AI Core behind get_recommendation — the prompt, the server‑side validation that guarantees the AI can only pick a real candidate, the single‑vs‑multi‑material sourcing logic, and how S/4 talks to BTP securely.

Have you added AI to a classic transaction — or is there a field in your world crying out for a smart default? Tell us in the comments where you'd inject this pattern next.

entry.title: Re: rowcnt cross-database
entry.content:
Since the rowcnt() function was deprecated with the introduction of ASE 15.0 I'm going to assume OP is running ASE 12.x in which case I'd suggest a global stored procedure (defined in the sybsystemprocs database with a name that starts with 'sp_' - though I'd suggest 'sp__' to distinguish from system stored procedures).

---------------------

For demo purposes I've created MyObject (table in db1; procedure in db2) :

use db1
go

create table MyObject
(a    int     null
,b    int     null
)
go

use db2
go

create procedure MyObject
as
    print 'hi'
go

Running the following query in both databases to obtain details on MyObject :

select  db_name() as 'database',name as 'object name',id,type
from    sysobjects
where   id = object_id('MyObject')
go

-- results reformatted for readability

 database object name id         type
 -------- ----------- ---------- ----
 db1      MyObject    1657105963 U
 db2      MyObject    1408005016 P

 We'll incorporate this same code in a global procedure (sp__help) we'll place in the sybsystemprocs database :

use sybsystemprocs
go

create procedure sp__help
@objname varchar(255) ='sysobject'
as
    select  db_name() as 'database',name as 'object name',id,type
    from    sysobjects
    where   id = object_id(@objname)
go

For demo purposes we'll make our calls to sp__help from the master database :

use master
go

exec db1..sp__help 'MyObject'
exec db2..sp__help 'dbo.MyObject'
go

 database object name      id         type 
 -------- ---------------- ---------- ---- 
 db1      MyObject         1657105963 U    

 database object name      id         type 
 -------- ---------------- ---------- ---- 
 db2      MyObject         1408005016 P

Notice that we use the database name (db1, db2) to fully qualify the stored proc name (as opposed to fully qualifying the object name as in OP's sample query).

NOTES:

  • while the above code was tested on an ASE 16.0 SP04 PL04 instance, I would expect it to also work on ASE 12.x
  • if there's a requirement to capture the global procedure's output for further T-SQL processing (eg, capture the row count result from OP's query), the global procedure can be modified to include output parameters [I'll leave this for OP to test]

entry.title: SAP Enterprise Service Management Q3 2026 Innovation Highlights
entry.content:
As SAP's Autonomous Enterprise vision continues to take shape across our portfolio, in Q3 2026 we delivered powerful new capabilities for SAP Enterprise Service Management (SAP ESM) customers, partners, and practitioners. Whether you are modernizing HR service delivery, managing financial shared services, or looking to drive higher self-service adoption across the enterprise and every business function, the Q3 2026 release has something for you.

Before we dive in, we’re excited to share our customers’ value stories! Take a moment to register for our upcoming webinars and hear about our customers’ deployment journeys and value achieved from a unified, AI led, shared service operations with SAP ESM.

🚀Tuesday, November 10, 2026
Cracking the Code on HR Service Delivery: Enercon's Journey
Featuring Enercon and their journey in unifying HR shared service delivery moderated by  HR Tech analyst,  Anita Lettnik.
Register here.
 
🚀Thursday, November 19, 2026
Smarter, Faster, Unified: SAP’s Journey to AI-Powered Shared Services
SAP’s global deployment with over 4000 service professionals live today, serving employees, partners and customers across XX business functions.
Register here.

Now, let’s dive into the Q3 2026 innovation highlights including insights on autonomous assistants coming your way!  For even more detailed insights on our Q3 2026 service innovations, register here for the Q3 2026 Release Overview on November 5th hosted by our product management team.

Intelligent case flow: Less effort with faster resolution

Case management in SAP ESM has proven to deliver the flexibility organizations need to model their shared service processes across the enterprise, coordinating complex workflows between automation and human action. The Q3 2026 enhancements to Case Flow reduce manual steps for both service representatives and administrators, allowing structured service processes to progress more naturally and more efficiently without unnecessary intervention.

Auto Complete Conditions for Input Steps in Case Flow

Input steps within a case flow allow service representatives to capture or update structured data in context without navigating away from the case. Until now, however, marking an input step as complete was always a manual action, even when the required conditions were clearly satisfied.

With this Q3 2026 release, administrators can now define conditions under which an input step will automatically mark itself as complete. When those conditions are met, for example, when specific field values have been set or when a case reaches a particular status, the system evaluates the configured logic and completes the step without requiring a service representative to take action.

Why it matters:

  • High-volume, structured processes benefit most. Think onboarding workflows, procurement inquiries, or HR case handling where multiple input steps follow predictable completion patterns.
  • Service representatives can focus on the steps that genuinely require their judgment, rather than clicking through steps the system can already identify as complete.
  • Administrators retain full control over when auto-completion applies, using the same familiar condition builder available throughout the Case Designer.

Auto Trigger for Case Approval Step

Approval steps in SAP ESM case flows are a critical governance mechanism, ensuring that key decisions are reviewed by the right people before a case proceeds. However, a common source of delay in approval-heavy workflows is simply that service representatives forget, or are too busy, to manually submit the approval request.

This enhancement allows administrators to configure an approval step to auto-submit as soon as its preconditions are met. Once the case reaches the configured state and all entry conditions are satisfied, the approval request is triggered automatically, without service representative intervention.

Why it matters:

  • Eliminates a common bottleneck in approval-gated workflows, particularly in financial shared services and compliance-driven processes where timely approvals are essential.
  • Works alongside existing precondition configuration, giving administrators precise control over when auto-submission is appropriate.
  • Approvers still receive requests and must act. This feature automates the submission, not the decision itself.

Accelerate Financial Service Delivery with Contract Accounts

For organizations delivering financial shared services, whether handling billing inquiries, payment disputes, collection workloads, or contract account management, having complete financial context within the service case is not a nice-to-have; it is essential. The Q3 2026 release introduces a deeply integrated Contract Account View, connecting SAP ESM directly to SAP Cloud ERP FI-CA financial data and bringing it into the agent's hands without the need to switch systems.

Contract Account View: Financial Documents, Invoices, Payments, and Collections

Service representatives working on financial inquiries can now see a complete picture of the customer's financial position right from the ESM agent desktop, without navigating to SAP Cloud ERP transaction screens. These include:

Financial Documents and Open Items: All FI-CA transactions for the past 365 days (configurable) are displayed, aggregated by document number.

Invoices: The last 12 months of invoices, billing documents, and billing plans are available, each with a direct link to the PDF printout.

Payments: All payment documents posted in the last 365 days are visible with real-time, color-coded status tags.

Collections: The full collections history from SAP Cloud ERP FI-CA is surfaced directly in ESM, covering dunning records, returns, and write-offs.

Contract Account View: Payment Arrangements, Locks, and Correspondence

Beyond raw financial data, the Contract Account View also provides service representatives with the context needed to understand active agreements, account restrictions, and prior correspondence, all without leaving the service agent desktop.

Payment Arrangements: All Promise to Pay agreements and Installment Plans for the contract account are visible in either card or table format.

Locks: Active and expired locks applied to the contract account are displayed, including lock type, reason, and date range.

Correspondences and Bank Data: Complete correspondence history, key attributes, and bank data, available in a dedicated tab.

This provides service representatives with a comprehensive financial picture in one place.

Elevating the self-service experience

The self-service application is how employees experience enterprise service management directly. Two Q3 2026 enhancements give administrators more precise control over what employees see and how they interact with their cases, resulting in a cleaner, more focused experience and fewer unnecessary support contacts.

Controlled Case Visibility in List View

In organizations where SAP ESM supports multiple lines of business, not every case type is intended for employee self-service visibility. With this Q3 2026 update, a new attribute has been added to the case type configuration to specify self-service relevance. Only cases belonging to case types that have been marked as self-service relevant in Case Type Configuration will appear in the employee's list. Cases associated with internal, service representative-only, or back-office case types will not be visible in the self-service interface.

Why it matters:

  • Employees see only the cases that are relevant and actionable for them, reducing confusion and erroneous selection.
  • Administrators gain precise control over the self-service experience, aligning what employees see with the organization's service delivery model.
  • This is particularly valuable for organizations running ESM across multiple functions such as HR, Finance, IT, and Procurement, where different case types serve very different audiences.

Enhanced Case Communication History

Understanding the full history of a case, including who said what, when, and through which channel, is fundamental to the self-service experience. Before this release, timeline events and case conversations were combined in a single Conversations tab, which made it harder to quickly locate a particular event or communication.

This enhancement restructures how case history is presented in the self-service interface, making it easier to locate specific events and communications, reducing inquiries back to the service representative and improving resolution times.

Why it matters:

  • A dedicated Timeline tab now presents all case events in chronological order, including status changes, assignments, workflow transitions, and other system-level activities, giving employees a clear audit trail of everything that has happened on their case.
  • The Conversations tab has been refined to focus on actual communications. A new Past Conversations section surfaces all non-internal notes, providing employees with a clear record of the dialogue between them and the service team.
  • Internal notes intended only for service representatives remain hidden from the employee-facing view, ensuring operational transparency is maintained without exposing confidential service team communications.

Preview: Autonomous Assistants

One of the most exciting themes at SAP SAPPHIRE and SAP Connect was the emergence of autonomous, AI-led assistants within SAP ESM. These are not incremental improvements to existing features; they represent a fundamentally different way of working, where Joule Work takes on complex, multi-step service and finance tasks with contextual intelligence and minimal human intervention. We are pleased to share an early look at two assistants currently progressing through Early Adopter Care, with general availability coming soon.

Recurring Receivables Assistant

Managing recurring revenue operations at scale is complex. Collections specialists, invoicing teams, subscription managers, and accounts receivable clerks each work within their own slice of a highly interconnected process, and when an exception occurs, resolving it typically requires manual coordination across multiple systems and stakeholders.

The Recurring Receivables Assistant coordinates execution across subscription orders and contracts, invoices, disputes, payments, and collections. The assistant helps teams prioritize collections, manage subscription contract changes, correct invoices, and resolve customer disputes and payments across multiple applications and solutions with clearer issue context and faster customer communication.

The assistant supports the core business stages across the receivables lifecycle:

  • Prioritize: Surfaces high-impact accounts, explains risk drivers, and recommends the next-best collection action, so collections specialists focus effort where it matters most.
  • Prevent: Detects invoice rejection risk before downstream impact occurs, identifies likely root causes, and recommends corrections, reducing exceptions before they slow collections.
  • Correct: Identifies contract data issues, validates corrections, simulates billing impact, and guides subscription specialists through the update, unblocking invoice and payment flow.
  • Resolve: Investigates payment exceptions and unmatched payments, connects invoice and contract context, and guides AR clerks through resolution, closing issues with less manual investigation.

Case Management Assistant

Every service representative manages cases, but the experience of working through a complex, multi-step case, coordinating with customers, extracting information from attachments, triggering backend processes, and knowing what to do next, can still be demanding and time-consuming. The Case Management Assistant is designed to change that.

Available as a standalone starting point for a service interaction or embedded directly in the SAP ESM agent desktop, the Case Management Assistant is a Joule-powered AI agent that works alongside service representatives throughout the full case lifecycle. 

Key dimensions of the assistant's capability include:

  • Contextual guidance: The assistant understands where a case is in its workflow and surfaces relevant next steps, so service representatives spend less time figuring out what to do and more time doing it.
  • Document and entity extraction: Attachments, emails, and case descriptions are automatically analyzed to extract key information, reducing manual data entry and improving case accuracy from the outset.
  • Communication assistance: Service representatives receive assistance drafting and refining customer communications within the case, ensuring timely and consistent responses that reflect the service organization's standards.
  • Connected process execution: The assistant can trigger actions in connected SAP systems, such as SAP Cloud ERP, directly from the case context, without requiring service representatives to navigate to separate applications.

Early adopter customers are actively engaged, already reporting measurable reductions in service representative effort.  Stay tuned for the general availability announcement, coming soon.

entry.title: Stop Building SAP Apps: Business AI Applications On Demand with an Ontology-Based MCP Server
entry.content:
Apps on demand instead of app projects

A sales rep desk for delivery-blocked orders on SAP ECC took us a few hours to build, not a project. It runs on live SAP data, follows the team's process step by step and writes back to SAP only after the rep confirms.

The usual route looks different. A new cockpit for one team starts a cycle of requirements, functional and technical specifications, OData services, a Fiori or UI5 front end, testing and transports. Weeks pass, and the team keeps working in reports, spreadsheets and email.

We took a typical wholesale scenario, connected Claude Desktop to the Skybuffer AI MCP server, our ABAP add-on, and asked for the application with nothing but the process description. This post shows what came out, the two architectures it runs on, and why the MCP server, more than the AI model, decides whether this works.

The example: a release desk for delivery block 17

The desk works the orders that SAP holds on delivery block 17 ("CSR action: deadline") because their cancel date is close. Each one needs a decision before that date, and the desk takes the customer service rep through all eight steps of the process on one screen, with live SAP data at every step.

The worklist: twelve orders on block 17, sorted by days to the cancel date, with stock coverage per order and a count of orders at each step.

StepWhat the rep sees and doesSkybuffer AI MCP tool
1. IdentifyEvery open order on the block, sorted by days left to the cancel date, with filters for overdue, due within two days and ready to releaseget_blocked_sales_orders
2. Check stockPer line: ordered quantity, available to promise, shortfall and the next incoming receipt; stock on hand per plantget_blocked_sales_orders, get_material_stock
3. DecideSAP's recommendation (release, extend, partial ship or cancel) with a plain-language reason; the rep makes the callget_blocked_sales_orders
4. Contact the customerOne email draft per customer, addressed to the buyer from SAP, covering all of their orders on hold with PO numbers, account executive in copyget_customers_contact_details
5. Customer replyThe answer is logged with a note, and a reply-by date drives a follow-up list(kept by the app)
6. Update SAPNew requested date, rejected lines with a reason, block kept or removed; every change shown in a confirmation dialog first, then read back from SAPchange_sales_order, get_sales_order_status
7. ReleaseBlock 17 removed, the order goes to the warehousechange_sales_order
8. Follow upOrders without an answer by the reply date come back as a chase list(kept by the app)

Steps 2 and 3: availability per line, stock on hand and SAP's recommendation with its reason. Here SAP suggests a partial shipment, and the rep picks the line to cancel.

When stock covers every line before the cancel date, SAP recommends a release instead. The customer doesn't need to hear from us, so the desk skips the email and lets the rep remove the block straight away.

Every line is available before the cancel date, so SAP suggests a release and no customer contact is needed.

Nobody wrote UI code by hand. Claude Desktop generated the application from the eight-step process description and the tool descriptions the MCP server publishes. The first version ran within a few hours of the first prompt, and we refined it over the same day.

Two rules held throughout. Nothing changes in SAP without the rep's confirmation, and customer emails are only drafted, never sent by the app.

Step 4: one draft per customer for all of their orders on hold, with the buyer's address from SAP and the account executive in copy. Nothing is sent from the page.

Step 6: before posting, the rep sees each change in plain words and the exact MCP call behind it.

Why the MCP server needs a business ontology, not an OData wrapper

The model can only build an app as good as the tools it is given. An MCP server that wraps OData services hands the model database entities; an MCP server built on a business ontology hands it the process itself.

By ontology we mean the shared vocabulary of the business: the objects (customer, sales order, line, delivery block, cancel date, availability, inbound receipt), how they relate, the actions allowed on them and the rules behind those actions. When the tools speak that vocabulary, the steps of the app can match the steps of the process one to one.

 OData wrapperBusiness ontology MCP server
A tool representsAn entity set: order headers, items, schedule linesA business capability: find blocked orders and assess them against their cancel date
Who joins the dataThe model, call by call: header, items, schedule lines, availability, stock listThe server, inside SAP, in one call
Business rulesRebuilt by the model each time: confirmations, rejected lines, units of measureImplemented once in ABAP with standard BAPIs
What comes backRaw fields such as VDATU, LIFSK, KWMENGAnswer-ready fields: days to cancel, coverage, next inbound date, recommended action and its reason
WritesA generic update on an entity; the model must know update flags and schedule linesBusiness actions: move the requested date and keep the block, reject lines with a reason, remove the block
AuthorizationsPer servicePer action and per order, checked against the user's SAP roles on every call

The difference shows in the numbers. The desk's worklist of twelve orders, with availability per line and a recommendation per order, comes from a single call. Built on entity reads, the same screen needs several reads per order plus an availability check per line, and every join is a chance for the model to get it wrong.

Every call goes to the live system, so the app works in real time. Nothing is replicated into a data lake or a side database, and SAP stays the system of record.

Architecture 1: the ABAP add-on and Claude Desktop

The simplest setup has two parts: Claude Desktop on the user's machine and the Skybuffer AI MCP server, installed as an ABAP add-on in the SAP system itself.

Architecture 1: Claude Desktop and the ABAP MCP add-on

The rep works in Claude Desktop and signs in to SAP through SSO with their own SAP user, so there is no shared technical user. Every tool call goes over HTTPS to the add-on, which runs the business logic inside SAP with standard BAPIs and checks that user's SAP authorizations before it returns or changes anything.

The add-on's MCP endpoint is an ICF node in the SAP system. Claude reaches it as a remote MCP connector, and connector calls come from Claude's cloud, so the ICF node is published through your reverse proxy or a secure tunnel; in Architecture 2, the gateway takes that role.

There is no middleware to install, no data replication and no separate app server. The add-on runs on SAP ECC and on SAP S/4HANA, with S/4HANA variants where the data model differs, so the app moves with the system through a migration.

This setup suits pilots, departmental apps and any team that wants the shortest path from an idea to a working app.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Companies that standardize on SAP BTP can put the MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, announced at SAP TechEd 2025, between Claude and the add-on. The app and the tools stay exactly the same; the gateway adds central governance.

Architecture 2: SAP BTP with the MCP Gateway in the middle

Claude calls the gateway with the user's identity. The gateway applies its policies and forwards the call through SAP Cloud Connector, and the add-on runs the same tools as in Architecture 1.

What the SAP-endorsed path adds, as SAP's reference architecture describes it:

  • One governed entry point for MCP tools, including external MCP servers such as the Skybuffer AI add-on
  • OAuth 2.0 and OIDC enforcement, rate limiting, payload protection and traffic management
  • Monitoring, distributed tracing and analytics in one place
  • Tool lifecycle from creation to versioning and deprecation, with MCP specification upgrades handled by SAP

The SAP system itself stays behind the firewall: SAP Cloud Connector opens an outbound tunnel to BTP, so no inbound port is needed.

The gateway can also turn existing APIs and integration flows into MCP tools. That is handy for simple reads, but for a process like this one it brings back the OData-wrapper problem. The split that works: the gateway governs the call, and the business ontology lives in the MCP server behind it.

The Skybuffer AI MCP server and its predefined tools

Both architectures run on the same MCP server: the Skybuffer AI MCP server, an ABAP add-on from Skybuffer that implements MCP inside SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA. It is built on SAP technology only, so any SAP team or partner can support it.

Out of the box, the server comes with predefined business tools. Each one is a business capability, such as reading a customer's contacts, checking stock or creating a purchase requisition, written in ABAP on a common framework and published with a description that tells the model when and how to use it.

Predefined tools are why an app takes hours instead of weeks:

  • Most of the app already exists. The desk reuses predefined tools for customer contacts, stock, order status and governed data access. Only two tools were new for this scenario, get_blocked_sales_orders and change_sales_order, and both are now part of the standard content.
  • Business logic is built once, tested and shared. Availability, confirmations, rejection reasons and units of measure are handled in ABAP with standard BAPIs instead of being reinvented by the model in every app. Two apps never disagree about the same order, and an improvement to a tool reaches every app that uses it.
  • Security comes with every call. Each tool checks the user's SAP authorizations before it reads or changes anything, and changes are recorded in the SAP application log. A new app inherits these controls instead of rebuilding them.
  • IT stays in control. Customizing decides which tools are active and which tables and views the data access tool may read, each with its own field list and record limit.

When a process needs something new, the new tool is one more ABAP class on the same framework, registered in customizing and transported like any other ABAP change. The server publishes it to every MCP client automatically, so the next app can use it the same day.

Distributing the app across the company

The desk is a published page on claude.ai, so rolling it out means sharing a link, not deploying an application. Claude artifacts on Team and Enterprise plans provide everything the rollout needs.

  1. Each user connects the Skybuffer AI connector once in Claude, under Settings > Connectors, and signs in through SSO with their own SAP user.
  2. The author shares the page with named colleagues or with the whole organization. Viewers sign in to Claude, on the desktop app or the web.
  3. An Owner keeps control in the admin settings: artifacts on or off, connector calls from artifacts on or off, and public sharing, which is off by default.

Once shared, these rules hold:

  • Every viewer sees their own SAP. Each connector call runs through the viewer's own connection, so two reps with different SAP roles see different orders. The page never sees credentials, and each viewer approves access before the first call.
  • Actions run as the person who clicks. A release, a new date or a rejected line is posted under that user's SAP account and authorizations.
  • The team shares one picture. Decisions, customer replies, notes and the activity feed are kept with the app, while SAP data is read live for each viewer.
  • Updates reach everyone. Each republish becomes a new version on the same link, and the owner chooses which version viewers see.
  • Governance is built in. Artifacts are visible only to signed-in members of the organization and the people they are shared with, and they fall under retention policies, the audit log and the Compliance API.

Conclusion: fast, cheap and built to SAP standards

With a proper MCP server and Claude Desktop, a business AI app stops being a project. A team describes its process in the morning and works in the app in the afternoon, on live SAP data.

 Classic app projectBusiness AI app on demand
First versionWeeks of specification, development and testingA few hours
Built byA development teamA consultant or power user with Claude Desktop
New to deployOData services, a Fiori or UI5 app, transportsNothing, once the add-on is in place: the app is a shared link
Fit to the processAs specified at the startBuilt from the process description, refined the same day
DataOften copied for reportingLive from SAP ECC or S/4HANA
A changeA change requestA prompt, republished to the same link

Fast. Apps arrive in hours, and changes the same day.

Cheap. Architecture 1 needs no middleware and no extra runtime, only the ABAP add-on in the existing system and Claude for the users. There is no UI code or OData layer to maintain, most tools come predefined with the server, and each new one is reused by the next app.

Very good quality. The logic runs in SAP through standard BAPIs and SAP authorization checks. Every change is confirmed by a person and read back, and the app follows the process because it was built from it.

The same approach works on SAP ECC today and on SAP S/4HANA after the migration. The Skybuffer AI MCP server is not tied to one client either: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and VS Code can all use the same tools. Start with Architecture 1 for speed, and move to Architecture 2 when the rollout needs SAP BTP governance.

entry.title: Clean Start Validation: How to Prevent Poor-Quality Email Addresses Entering Your List at Sign-Up
entry.content:
Why Email Sign-Up Data Quality Matters

This article describes the Clean Start Validation approach — a set of email address validation methods applied at the point of sign-up to prevent poor-quality data from entering a mailing list. It is intended for email marketers and deliverability teams who want to improve list quality, protect sender reputation, and reduce compliance risk from the point of first contact.

Poor-quality subscriber data is one of the most persistent problems in email marketing. Once invalid or inactive addresses enter a mailing list, they are difficult to identify and remove without also discarding genuinely inactive but real customers. The most effective solution is to prevent low-quality addresses from being added in the first place.

Several factors make this more urgent today:

  • Mailbox providers — such as Gmail, Microsoft/Outlook, and Yahoo — are stricter with senders who have poor data quality or low engagement rates.
  • List-bombing attacks — where automated systems submit large numbers of fake or temporary email addresses to sign-up forms — are increasing in frequency.
  • Once invalid data is in a mailing list, it is difficult to distinguish between genuinely inactive customers and so-called "zombie" addresses: contacts that appear active but provide no real engagement value.
  • Data protection regulations, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) Article 5(1)(d), require that personal data be accurate, kept up to date, and that inaccurate data be removed promptly.
  • Removing old and inactive contacts from a list — known as sunsetting — is an important ongoing hygiene practice, but it does not solve the root problem: it addresses data already on the list, not data entering it.

By focusing on validation earlier in the data lifecycle — at the moment of sign-up — senders can build healthier lists, improve campaign results, and reduce the risk of long-term deliverability and compliance issues.

Why Privacy Features Are Increasing the Risk of Inactive and Misleading Contacts

Recent changes in email privacy technology have made traditional engagement tracking methods less reliable. Features designed to protect user privacy — including Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP), Apple's "Hide My Email" service, and Google's forthcoming "Shielded Email" feature — can generate artificial engagement signals, particularly automatic email opens, that do not reflect genuine recipient activity.

These features, combined with the already widespread availability of temporary email address services from some mailbox providers, are increasing the likelihood of zombie addresses appearing on mailing lists. These are contacts that appear to engage — for example, through automatically generated opens — but provide no real value. They stagnate in lists and skew performance metrics, making it harder for senders to accurately measure campaign effectiveness or identify genuinely disengaged recipients.

Why Validating Email Addresses at Sign-Up Protects Deliverability and Engagement

Validating email addresses at the point of sign-up — before they are added to the mailing list — allows senders to identify and block low-quality addresses before they can affect deliverability or engagement metrics.

By catching invalid, inactive, or temporary addresses early, email marketers can:

  • Prevent low-quality data from affecting email deliverability.
  • Identify the risk of bot attacks and automated spam sign-ups quickly.
  • Ensure messages reach real, engaged recipients.
  • Improve return on investment (ROI) through better campaign results at lower send volumes.
  • Reduce compliance risk under data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

Why Most Recipients Who Mark Your Email as Spam Will Remain on Your List

Gmail, iCloud, and the default mail applications on Android and iOS do not send feedback loop unsubscribe requests to senders when a recipient marks an email as junk or spam. This means that when a recipient marks a message as spam, the sender is not notified and the contact is not automatically removed from the mailing list.

This creates a compounding problem. If the original delivery of the email was recorded as an "open" — whether from a genuine read or an automatic open generated by Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) or a similar privacy feature — the sender may classify the contact as "active" for months or even years, continuing to send to someone who has already indicated they do not want the emails.

This makes preventing these contacts from entering the list in the first place even more important: once a low-quality or disengaged contact is on the list, there may be no reliable signal that they should be removed.

What the Rate of Inactive New Contacts Indicates About Sign-Up Quality

Based on deliverability reviews conducted by the Emarsys Deliverability team across a range of brand accounts, approximately 5–10% of new sign-ups typically remain completely inactive — showing no engagement in the period immediately following sign-up. This level is considered a normal baseline: genuine customers do not always engage with their first email immediately.

However, when the proportion of inactive new contacts exceeds 10%, this typically indicates a problem with sign-up quality. Common causes include:

  • Bot or automated sign-ups bypassing validation controls.
  • Insufficient validation allowing invalid or temporary addresses through.
  • Broken or unclear onboarding processes that fail to prompt new subscribers to engage.

By monitoring the percentage of new contacts who remain inactive after sign-up, email marketers can diagnose data quality issues early and refine their sign-up strategy before the problem scales.

How to Implement Clean Start Validation

A proactive approach to list quality begins at the point of sign-up. The goal of Clean Start Validation is to validate email addresses in real time and confirm their legitimacy before they can enter the mailing list and affect engagement metrics. Two complementary validation methods are recommended.

Real-Time Validation at Sign-Up

Implementing real-time validation at the point of entry — on sign-up forms, at eCommerce checkouts, and at any other point where email addresses are collected — allows senders to check address validity before the contact is added to the list. Real-time validation can identify:

  • Syntax errors and incorrectly formatted addresses.
  • Invalid or non-existent email domains.
  • Domains with no responding mail server.
  • Disposable or temporary email addresses.
  • Bot-generated sign-ups.

This is typically achieved using two categories of tool:

  • Email validation services — which check address syntax, domain validity, and mail server response in real time at the point of submission.
  • Bot prevention tools such as reCAPTCHA — which filter out automated sign-up attempts before they reach the validation step.

First-Click Validation and Double Opt-In

Two confirmation-based approaches verify that a submitted email address belongs to a real, active recipient:

First-click validation places a new subscriber in an "unverified" status until they click a confirmation link in a welcome email. Unlike open-tracking — which can produce false signals through automatic opens generated by Apple Mail Privacy Protection (MPP) and similar privacy features — first-click validation confirms that a real person has accessed their inbox and taken a deliberate action. Only verified contacts are moved to the main mailing list.

Double opt-in (DOI) is an established, widely recommended method that requires new subscribers to confirm their sign-up by clicking a link in a confirmation email before their address is added to the list. Double opt-in has some drawbacks — including a higher drop-off rate and slower list growth than single opt-in — but for senders who prioritise list quality over volume, it remains an effective way to ensure subscribers are genuinely interested and actively consenting.

Combining Real-Time Validation with Confirmation-Based Methods

Combining real-time validation with either first-click validation or double opt-in (DOI) creates a stronger, cleaner list from day one. Together, these methods:

  • Block invalid, bot-generated, and temporary email addresses at the point of entry.
  • Reduce the risk of zombie addresses accumulating on the list and skewing performance metrics.
  • Improve engagement rates and sender reputation by ensuring the active list consists of real, verified recipients.
  • Support compliance with data protection regulations by ensuring that contact data is accurate and that consent is confirmed at sign-up.

Summary: Build List Quality from the Point of Sign-Up

Email list hygiene is not only about removing inactive subscribers over time — it begins with preventing poor-quality data from entering the list in the first place.

The key considerations for senders are:

  • The problem is growing. Privacy-driven features from Apple and Google are increasing the proportion of artificial engagement signals, making it harder to identify genuinely inactive or invalid contacts after the fact.
  • Prevention is more effective than removal. Real-time validation at sign-up stops invalid and bot-generated addresses before they affect list quality or deliverability.
  • Confirmation methods provide an additional layer of protection. First-click validation and double opt-in (DOI) ensure that only real, inbox-active recipients are added to the main list.
  • Monitor new contact inactivity rates. Based on Emarsys Deliverability team observations, a rate above 10% for inactive new contacts is an early indicator of a sign-up quality problem that should be investigated.

Senders who implement Clean Start Validation — combining real-time validation with a confirmation-based method — can build more engaged subscriber lists, protect their sender reputation, and reduce both deliverability and compliance risk from day one.

So today I counted it in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, from the technical settings of the 296 custom transparent tables. Only 2 have log changes on with data class APPL0, which is the 0022 error, priority 1. Only 1 is a small table with buffering allowed but switched off, the 0003 warning. And 5 customizing tables (delivery class C) still have buffering not allowed, the 0010 case.

What surprised me was the other side: only 2 of the 296 tables have buffering switched on at all. Almost all of them are application tables (delivery class A), and 0010 doesn't look at those.

So for me the check is much quieter than its reputation. I would block the release on its priority 1 and 2 findings, because they are few and each one is a real decision, and go through the information messages once, table by table, instead of exempting them all.
